## Seven continents

<span class="k">Cologne → Germany → Europe → the world</span>

Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. That is what most of us learned.

<span class="chip">7 continents</span>

## There is an eighth.

Hiding in the South Pacific, about 18,000 km from this room: **Zealandia**.

<span class="chip">≈ 4.9 million km²</span><span class="chip">≈ 94% underwater</span><span class="chip">proposed, not yet official</span>

## Why call it a continent? {.wide}

- Raised above the surrounding ocean floor
- Distinct geology
- A well-defined area
- Thicker crust than the ocean floor

<span class="m">Criteria and figures: Mortimer et al. (2017)</span>

## What can you build with maps like this? {.full}

<span class="chip">Retail: where to open the next store</span><span class="chip">Logistics: the fastest delivery routes</span><span class="chip">Real estate: price maps by neighbourhood</span><span class="chip">Insurance: flood and storm risk zones</span><span class="chip">Health: how a disease spreads</span><span class="chip">Marketing: where your customers live</span>

Zealandia is one example. The method is the same everywhere: **data with a location, turned into a map**.

## Introducing the data {.full}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**GEBCO**: one global grid of elevation, land and sea floor.

Every **raster cell** stores a longitude, a latitude and **one value**: elevation in metres.

Positive = land. Negative = sea floor.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{=html}
<table class="grid">
<tr><td>-4200</td><td>-3900</td><td>-2600</td><td>-1800</td></tr>
<tr><td>-3800</td><td>-2400</td><td>-900</td><td>-300</td></tr>
<tr><td>-3500</td><td>-2100</td><td class="hi">120</td><td>640</td></tr>
<tr><td>-3300</td><td>-1900</td><td>310</td><td>1450</td></tr>
</table>
```
<span class="m">Teal cell: above sea level (an island). Cell size: 15 arc-seconds.</span>
:::
:::

## Live coding 1: load the data {.full}

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|2|3-6|7"}
library(terra)
files <- list.files("data", pattern = "\\.(tif|nc)$", full.names = TRUE)
tiles <- lapply(files, function(f) {
  r <- rast(f)                        # read the raster
  if (xmin(r) < 0) r <- shift(r, dx = 360)   # date line fix
  r })
elev <- if (length(tiles) == 1) tiles[[1]] else do.call(merge, tiles)
```

<span class="m">`rast()` reads a file as a raster. East of the date line longitudes are negative, so we shift them by 360° to get one continuous Pacific. `merge()` joins the tiles.</span>

## Live coding 2: process the raster {.full}

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|2-3"}
elev_s <- aggregate(elev, fact = 10, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
df <- as.data.frame(elev_s, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
names(df) <- c("lon", "lat", "elev")
```

<span class="m">Millions of cells are too many to plot: `aggregate()` averages 10 × 10 blocks. `as.data.frame(xy = TRUE)` gives one row per cell (lon, lat, elev), which is what `ggplot2` needs.</span>

## Live coding 3: the colour scale {.full}

<div class="bar"></div>
<div class="scale"><span>−10,500 m</span><span>−2,000</span><span>0 m (shoreline)</span><span>1,500</span><span>3,800 m</span></div>

```{.r}
br   <- c(-10500, -6000, -4000, -2000, -1000, -200, 0, 500, 1500, 3800)
cols <- c("#030b2e", "#0a2463", "#1b4f9c", "#2f80c9", "#5db0e6",
          "#b5e3f5", "#efe6b8", "#7fb069", "#a67c52", "#ffffff")
```

<span class="m">One colour per break; `ggplot2` blends in between. Sea and land get different hues, so 0 m is a clear coastline.</span>

## Live coding 4: build the map {.full}

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|3-4|5-6|7"}
ggplot(df, aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = elev)) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = cols, values = scales::rescale(br),
                       limits = range(br), oob = scales::squish) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = elev), breaks = c(-2500, 0), colour = "white") +
  coord_quickmap() +
  theme_minimal()
```

<span class="m">`geom_raster` paints each cell. `scale_fill_gradientn` applies our colours. `geom_contour` draws the 0 m coastline and the 2,500 m line. `coord_quickmap` keeps the map shape right.</span>

## Reading the map {.full}

```{r}
#| echo: false
if (file.exists("zealandia_map.png")) knitr::include_graphics("zealandia_map.png") else knitr::asis_output("*Run zealandia_gebco.R first: it creates zealandia_map.png.*")
```

<span class="chip">shallow platforms: pale blue</span><span class="chip">deep basins and trenches: dark blue</span><span class="chip">visible islands: beige to brown</span>

## The elevation distribution {.full}

```{r}
#| echo: false
if (file.exists("zealandia_hist.png")) knitr::include_graphics("zealandia_hist.png") else knitr::asis_output("*Run zealandia_gebco.R first: it creates zealandia_hist.png.*")
```

Two humps: **shallow platform** and **deep ocean floor**. Almost nothing near 0 m: a continent that is almost entirely submerged looks like a plateau, not like land.
